By Mike Allen · Aug 28, 2026

🥳 Happy Friday! Today's newsletter, edited by Alex Fitzpatrick, is 596 words, a 2-min. read. Thanks to Carolyn DiPaolo for copy editing.

⚡️ Situational awareness: In a much-anticipated speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh suggested that interest rate hikes are possible if inflation doesn't fall. More from Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown.
 
 
1 big thing: Roman ready for launch
 
A rendering of the Roman Space Telescope. Image: NASA

NASA is preparing to launch the Roman Space Telescope — one of the agency's biggest and most promising scientific endeavors in years, Alex Fitzpatrick reports.

🔭 Roman is designed to help answer some of science's most tantalizing mysteries, including questions around dark matter and dark energy.

  • Researchers also hope to use it to discover a plethora of new exoplanets — worlds outside our own solar system.

🚀 Launch is set for early Sunday from Florida's Kennedy Space Center aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket.

  • Roman is carrying two scientific devices: the Wide Field Instrument and the Coronagraph Instrument.

📸 The first is a 300-megapixel near-infrared camera with a field of view 100x that of the esteemed Hubble Space Telescope. The result: much faster data collection and discovery-making.

  • The second will be used for high-contrast imaging and spectroscopy of nearby exoplanets to better understand them. (Spectroscopy is a way of studying planets and other objects based on their color.)
Roman is lifted into a portable clean room called the "Chariot" for transportation ahead of launch. Photo: Sydney Rohde/NASA

🪐 Researchers hope that data from Roman can help answer lingering questions about two of the universe's least-understood phenomena: dark energy and dark matter.

  • Scientists have proposed dark energy as the driving force behind the universe's accelerating expansion.
  • Dark matter is thought to be an invisible "glue" binding the universe together.

🛰️ Jeff Kruk, Roman's deputy senior project scientist, tells Axios: "I can't help but think that the biggest result from Roman 10 years from now is something that we just haven't thought of yet."

2. 📈 Fastest-growing jobs
 
Data: BLS. Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

Health care and social assistance jobs are projected to see the most growth over the next decade, Axios' Emily Peck writes from a new government report.

🧑‍⚕️ There will be about 847,000 new home health and personal care aide jobs created from 2025 to 2035, the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects.

  • Other fields with big expected growth: registered nurses, health services managers and nurse practitioners.
  • That's fueled by America's aging population, which needs more care.

🤖 Yes, but: The report also forecasts job losses across several occupations as a result of AI and automation.

  • It projects about 752,000 fewer office and admin support jobs over the next decade, for example.

3. ⚡️ Catch me up
 
Satellite image ©2026 Vantor via AP
  1. 🛰️ New satellite images of Syapru Besi, Nepal, reveal the extent of the devastation caused by Wednesday's catastrophic flash flooding. Nearly 600 people died and almost 2,500 remain missing. Get the latest.
  2. 🧑‍⚖️ Jurors are still deliberating in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with killing her three children in 2023. Live updates.
  3. 🎧 Streams of Dolly Parton's music on Spotify have jumped over 2,000% in the U.S., and over 1,000% globally, since her death on Tuesday. Top songs: "Jolene" (1.3 million streams) and "9 to 5" (1.1 million), Axios Nashville's Adam Tamburin reports. Essential albums.
 
 
4. 🍦 1 food thing: Chicken salad cone, anyone?
 
The pickle pie wasn't for us, but we loved the Hmong corn dog and the savory cones. Photos: Audrey Kennedy/Axios

The chicken salad cones on offer at this year's Minnesota State Fair are a hit, Axios' Torey Van Oot, Kyle Stokes, Audrey Kennedy and Geoff Ziezulewicz report from their whirlwind food tour.

  • The Axios Twin Cities team writes: "We spent five hours braving the crowds, lines and calories to taste-test this year's buzziest and most intriguing new foods."
Torey, Geoff, Audrey and Kyle. Photo: Torey Van Oot/Axios

🌭 Their other must-tries: The Hmong corn dog, ube cheesecake wontons, cracklin' corn ribs, and elote tots.

  • Honorable mentions: Tanghulu (a candy-covered kabob), a mango sticky rice refresher, and jerk chicken loaded fries.
